title: Tool contracts
point: A tool contract is a name, a description, an argument schema and a typed result, and the description is a prompt the model reads to choose.
definition: A tool contract is the published interface of one tool: a unique name, a plain-language description, a JSON Schema for its arguments and a typed result. The model selects and fills a tool from the contract alone.

objective.text: Given a vague tool definition, rewrite its name, description and argument schema so a model selects it correctly, and list the typed results it can return.

misconceptions.claim: The description is documentation for humans, so a short phrase is enough.
misconceptions.correction: The model chooses tools from the description. A vague one, such as gets data, causes wrong selection, so write it as a prompt: when to use it, when not to, and what it returns.

misconceptions.claim: A JSON Schema for the arguments makes a tool safe to call.
misconceptions.correction: The schema checks shape, not intent or permission. A well-formed refund for the wrong order still passes, so authorisation and business rules belong in the gateway.

l1: A tool contract has four parts: a name, a description, a JSON Schema for the arguments and a typed result. The model reads the first three; the orchestrator relies on the fourth.
The description is effectively a prompt. The model reads it to decide whether the tool fits the task, so a vague description leads to the wrong tool being chosen.
The schema constrains arguments with types, required fields, enums and ranges. The typed result is SUCCESS, EMPTY, DENIED, UNAVAILABLE or INVALID, so no caller has to parse free text.
l2: Take a tool named get_data, described as gets customer data, with one free-text query argument. The model calls it for orders, invoices and profiles alike, and fills the query with guesses.
Rewrite it as get_order_status. The description says it returns the status and last update of one order by ID, and that it is not for refunds or invoices. The only argument is an order_id string.

The result is SUCCESS with a status and timestamp, EMPTY when no order matches, or INVALID when the ID breaks the pattern. The model now picks it only for order status and repairs malformed IDs itself.
l3: Every tool definition sits in the context of every model call. Forty tools at 150 tokens each add 6,000 input tokens to each call.
At 300 model calls a minute, that is 1.8 million tokens a minute spent on definitions. Trimming each definition to 80 tokens saves 2,800 tokens per call.
So spend description tokens where selection actually fails. Find the tools an eval set shows being confused with each other, and lengthen only those with a line saying when not to use them.
